plain_english:
Think about who you are. First, you're a human being. And humans have something special — the power to choose. This power of choice is superior to everything else. All other things serve it. And this power itself is free. No one can enslave it.

Think about what sets you apart because of your ability to reason. You're different from wild animals. You're different from farm animals. Beyond that, you're a citizen of the entire world. You're part of it — not as a servant, but as one of the ruling parts. You can understand how the universe works. You can see how everything connects.
original_excerpt: Consider who you are. In the first place, you are a man; and this is one who has nothing superior to the faculty of the will, but all other things subjected to it; and the faculty itself he possesses unenslaved and free from subjection. Consider then from what things you have been separated by reason. You have been separated from wild beasts; you have been separated from domestic animals ([Greek: probaton]). Further, you are a citizen of the world, and a part of it, not one of the subservient (serving), but one of the principal (ruling) parts, for you are capable of comprehending the divine administration and of considering the connection of things.
source_reference: Discourses, How We May Discover the Duties of Life from Names

plain_english: What does being a good citizen require? It means you don't think only about what benefits you personally. You don't make decisions as if you're separate from your community. Instead, you act like a hand or foot would act if it could think and understood how the body works — it would never move or want anything except what's good for the whole body. This is why philosophers say that if a good person knew the future, he would willingly accept his own illness, death, and injury. He would know these things are assigned to him by the universal order. The whole is more important than the part. The state is more important than the citizen. But since we can't know the future, we should stick to choosing things that are naturally better for us to choose. After all, we were made for this purpose among others.
original_excerpt: What then does the character of a citizen promise (profess)? To hold nothing as profitable to himself; to deliberate about nothing as if he were detached from the community, but to act as the hand or foot would do, if they had reason and understood the constitution of nature, for they would never put themselves in motion nor desire anything otherwise than with reference to the whole. Therefore, the philosophers say well, that if the good man had foreknowledge of what would happen, he would co-operate towards his own sickness and death and mutilation, since he knows that these things are assigned to him according to the universal arrangement, and that the whole is superior to the part, and the state to the citizen. But now because we do not know the future, it is our duty to stick to the things which are in their nature more suitable for our choice, for we were made among other things for this.
source_reference: Discourses, How We May Discover the Duties of Life from Names

plain_english: Remember that you are a son. What does being a son require? Think of everything you have as belonging to your father. Obey him in everything. Never badmouth him to others or say or do anything that hurts him. Give way to him in all things and cooperate with him as much as you can. Remember too that you are a brother. What does being a brother require? Make compromises. Be easy to convince. Speak well of your brother. Never fight him over things that aren't up to you anyway — just let him have them. Focus instead on what is up to you. Think about it: you might give up a head of lettuce or a chair, but you gain good character in return. What a bargain that is.
original_excerpt: After this, remember that you are a son. What does this character promise? To consider that everything which is the son's belongs to the father, to obey him in all things, never to blame him to another, nor to say or do anything which does him injury, to yield to him in all things and give way, co-operating with him as far as you can. After this know that you are a brother also, and that to this character it is due to make concessions; to be easily persuaded, to speak good of your brother, never to claim in opposition to him any of the things which are independent of the will, but readily to give them up, that you may have the larger share in what is dependent on the will. For see what a thing it is, in place of a lettuce, if it should so happen, or a seat, to gain for yourself goodness of disposition. How great is the advantage.
source_reference: Discourses, How We May Discover the Duties of Life from Names

plain_english: Remember your role. If you're a senator in any government, remember you're a senator. If you're young, remember you're young. If you're old, remember you're old. Each title comes with specific duties that you need to examine and understand. But if you go around criticizing your brother, I'm telling you: you've forgotten who you are and what you're supposed to be. Think about it this way. If you were a blacksmith and you used your hammer wrong, you'd have forgotten how to be a blacksmith. If you've forgotten how to be a brother and become an enemy instead, haven't you clearly traded one thing for another? And if instead of being a human — a civilized, social creature — you've become a harmful wild animal, sneaky and vicious, haven't you lost something important?
original_excerpt: Next to this, if you are a senator of any state, remember that you are a senator; if a youth, that you are a youth; if an old man, that you are an old man; for each of such names, if it comes to be examined, marks out the proper duties. But if you go and blame your brother, I say to you, You have forgotten who you are and what is your name. In the next place, if you were a smith and made a wrong use of the hammer, you would have forgotten the smith; and if you have forgotten the brother and instead of a brother have become an enemy, would you appear not to have changed one thing for another in that case? And if instead of a man, who is a tame animal and social, you are become a mischievous wild beast, treacherous, and biting, have you lost nothing?
source_reference: Discourses, How We May Discover the Duties of Life from Names

plain_english: But you think you must lose some money and suffer damage? Does losing anything else damage a person? If you lost your knowledge of grammar or music, would you call that damage? And if you lose your sense of shame, self-control, and gentleness — do you think losing those things is nothing? Here's the difference: you lose the first things (money, knowledge) because of outside forces beyond your control. You lose the second things (character traits) through your own fault. With the first group, having them or losing them isn't shameful. But with the second group — not having them and losing them is shameful, disgraceful, and truly unfortunate.
original_excerpt: But (I suppose) you must lose a bit of money that you may suffer damage? And does the loss of nothing else do a man damage? If you had lost the art of grammar or music, would you think the loss of it a damage? and if you shall lose modesty, moderation ([Greek: chtastolaen]) and gentleness, do you think the loss nothing? And yet the things first mentioned are lost by some cause external and independent of the will, and the second by our own fault; and as to the first neither to have them nor to lose them is shameful; but as to the second, not to have them and to lose them is shameful and matter of reproach and a misfortune.
source_reference: Discourses, How We May Discover the Duties of Life from Names

plain_english: What then? Should I hurt someone who hurt me? First, think about what "hurt" really means. Remember what the philosophers taught you. If good comes from your choices and evil comes from your choices too, then listen to what you're actually saying: "Since that person hurt himself by being unfair to me, should I hurt myself by being unfair back to him?" Why don't we think about it this way?
original_excerpt: What then? shall I not hurt him who has hurt me? In the first place consider what hurt ([Greek: blabae]) is, and remember what you have heard from the philosophers. For if the good consists in the will (purpose, intention, [Greek: proaireeis]), and the evil also in the will, see if what you say is not this: What then, since that man has hurt himself by doing an unjust act to me, shall I not hurt myself by doing some unjust act to him? Why do we not imagine to ourselves (mentally think of) something of this kind?
source_reference: Discourses, How We May Discover the Duties of Life from Names

plain_english: When your body gets hurt or you lose your possessions, you call that harm. But when your will gets corrupted — when you're deceived or do something unjust — you think that's no harm at all. The person who lies or acts unfairly doesn't get a headache or lose their house. And those are the only things we care about protecting. We don't care whether our will becomes decent and trustworthy, or shameless and unreliable. We only worry about that in school, and only with a few fancy words. So our progress stops at those few words. Beyond that, we make no real progress at all.
original_excerpt: But where there is any detriment to the body or to our possession, there is harm there; and where the same thing happens to the faculty of the will, there is (you suppose) no harm; for he who has been deceived or he who has done an unjust act neither suffers in the head nor in the eye nor in the hip, nor does he lose his estate; and we wish for nothing else than (security to) these things. But whether we shall have the will modest and faithful or shameless and faithless, we care not the least, except only in the school so far as a few words are concerned. Therefore our proficiency is limited to these few words; but beyond them it does not exist even in the slightest degree.
source_reference: Discourses, How We May Discover the Duties of Life from Names
